title: Bahrain | CBB Financial Crime (Module FC) and AML Law Compliance
tagline: Bahrain's AML law and the CBB's Module FC in practice: CDD, PEPs, STRs to the FIU, sanctions, the MLRO and records.
sectors: Conventional banks licensed by the Central Bank of Bahrain
Correspondent banking, payments and trade finance
description:
A country-specific quest for staff of **conventional banks licensed by the Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB)**. It is built on **Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001** on the prevention and prohibition of money laundering, as amended (including **Decree-Law No. 36 of 2017** on terrorist financing), the CBB's **Financial Crime Module (Module FC) in Volume 1 of the CBB Rulebook**, the CBB's guidance on risk assessment, terrorist financing and beneficial ownership, and reporting to the financial intelligence unit at the Ministry of Interior.

Module FC content comes from **CBB-hosted copies** that could be opened: the 2023 copies issued with the Module FC amendments, and an earlier CBB-hosted consultation copy used only for sections whose 'date last changed' matches the 2023 contents list. The in-force Rulebook site could not be opened, so always check the current paragraph. Volume 1 only: other Rulebook volumes are not covered.

It is for branch, onboarding, payments, monitoring, correspondent and trade staff, the MLRO team, managers and board members who need to know the offences, the risk-based approach, CDD and enhanced due diligence, PEPs, STRs and tipping off, sanctions in general terms, the MLRO, records and the CBB's enforcement powers.

This quest builds knowledge of the Bahrain framework; it does not replace your institution's own AML/CFT policies and procedures, which you must always follow.
audience: Employees of CBB-licensed conventional banks who need a grounding in Bahrain's AML law and Module FC
Branch, call-centre and onboarding staff who identify customers and handle cash and transfers
Transaction monitoring, payments, correspondent banking and trade finance teams
MLROs, deputy MLROs and compliance staff preparing for CBB AML/CFT examinations
Senior managers and board members accountable for the bank's AML/CFT systems and controls
outcomes: Explain the money laundering, related and terrorist financing offences under Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001 as amended, and banks' Article 5 duties
Apply the CBB's risk-based approach and Module FC's CDD, beneficial ownership, timing and monitoring rules
Apply enhanced due diligence for PEPs, non-residents, correspondents, introduced business and wire transfers
Escalate suspicion to the MLRO, support an online STR to the FIU and the CBB, and avoid tipping off
Describe in general terms the duties to screen, freeze and report for UN and CBB-designated persons
Describe the MLRO's role, board oversight, record keeping and the CBB's enforcement powers

quest.name: Guardians of the Bay
quest.premise: You have just joined the Financial Crime Compliance team of Pearlgate Bank, a fictional conventional retail and wholesale bank licensed by the CBB, with its head office at Bahrain Bay in Manama and branches in Muharraq and Riffa. The CBB's Compliance Directorate has announced an onsite AML/CFT examination. With MLRO Noora Al Mahmood, branch manager Yusuf Janahi, analyst Anjali Menon and correspondent banking head David Okafor, clear five stages, then face the final boss: briefing chief executive Khalid Al Mannai and the board.

sessions.title: Bahrain's Framework: Decree-Law 4 of 2001, the CBB and Module FC
sessions.summary: Map Bahrain's anti-money laundering framework: Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001 and its amendments, the money laundering and related offences, the duties it places on banks, the authorities involved and how the CBB's Financial Crime Module for conventional banks fits on top.
objectives: Describe the money laundering offence, the related offences and corporate liability under Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001
List the duties Article 5 of the Decree-Law places on banks and explain why secrecy cannot be pleaded
Explain the roles of the CBB, the Ministry of Interior's financial intelligence unit, the Policy Committee and the Public Prosecution
Explain how Module FC in Volume 1 of the CBB Rulebook applies to conventional banks and which version this quest uses

cards.title: Day one at Pearlgate Bank
cards.setting: Financial Crime Compliance floor, Pearlgate Bank head office, Bahrain Bay, Manama. 8:30 am.

lines.text: Your badge photo is slightly blurred, but it opens the door. A note on your desk says: 'Welcome. Meeting room 4 at 9. Bring questions.'
Good morning, and welcome to Pearlgate. I'm Noora Al Mahmood, the bank's MLRO. You'll be shadowing me for a while.
Timing is lively: the CBB's Compliance Directorate has told us it plans an onsite AML/CFT examination of the bank.
(on a video call from Muharraq branch) Yusuf here. My tellers ask me whether money laundering is a police matter or something we answer for.
And my monitoring team wants to know which rules our alerts are really built on: the law, the Rulebook or our own policy.
All fair questions. Before we look at a single customer, everyone needs the same map: the law, the regulator's rules and who does what.
Stage one is the Bahrain Bay Tower. Climb it with me and you'll have answers for both of them by lunch.

cards.title: Bahrain's AML framework in five scenes

scenes.heading: The law at the base
scenes.narration: Decree-Law Number 4 of 2001 is Bahrain's anti-money laundering law. It creates the money laundering offence, related offences and penalties, and lists the core duties of institutions such as banks.

scenes.heading: Amended over time
scenes.narration: The law has been amended since 2001. A 2017 amendment, Decree-Law Number 36, rewrote the terrorist financing offence in Article 3 and set heavy penalties for it.

scenes.heading: The regulator's rules
scenes.narration: The Central Bank of Bahrain licenses and supervises banks. For conventional banks, its detailed AML and CFT rules sit in the Financial Crime Module, called Module FC, in Volume 1 of the CBB Rulebook.

scenes.heading: Where suspicions go
scenes.narration: Suspicious transaction reports go to the financial intelligence unit at the Ministry of Interior, which the law calls the Enforcement Unit, and, under Module FC, also to the CBB's Compliance Directorate.

scenes.heading: Policy and prosecution
scenes.narration: A national Policy Committee sets general anti-money laundering policy and reporting guidelines, and the Public Prosecution brings money laundering cases before the courts.

cards.title: Layers of Bahrain's AML/CFT framework
cards.caption: Each layer must fit the one above it. Your bank's procedures are where the rules meet real customers.

items.label: Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001
items.detail: The AML law, as amended: offences, penalties, institutions' duties and the authorities' powers.

items.label: CBB Law of 2006
items.detail: Gives the CBB power to issue binding directives to its licensees and to enforce them.

items.label: Module FC, Volume 1
items.detail: The CBB's directive for conventional banks: CDD, monitoring, MLRO, STRs, records and sanctions.

items.label: CBB guidance papers
items.detail: Risk assessment, terrorist financing, beneficial ownership and other guidance read with Module FC.

items.label: Pearlgate's own policies
items.detail: Board-approved procedures that turn all of the above into daily steps.

cards.title: Who does what in Bahrain?
cards.prompt: Match each body to its role in the anti-money laundering system.

pairs.right: Runs AML/CFT examinations of licensees, issues AML/CFT rules and guidance and receives copies of STRs

pairs.left: FIU at the Ministry of Interior
pairs.right: Receives and analyses reports of suspected money laundering and can investigate and seek court orders
Sets general anti-money laundering policies and issues guidelines on suspicious transaction reporting
Brings money laundering and related cases before the courts
The regional FATF-style body; Bahrain is a founding member and hosts its secretariat

cards.question: A customer was never convicted of the fraud that produced his funds. Can he still be convicted of laundering them under Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001?
options: No, the predicate offence must be proved in court first
Yes, the law allows a money laundering conviction without a conviction for the underlying crime
Only if the fraud took place inside Bahrain
Only if the bank filed an STR before the arrest
cards.explanation: The Decree-Law states that a person can be punished for money laundering even if not convicted of the underlying criminal activity, and 'criminal activity' covers crimes in Bahrain or in any other state.

cards.title: What the Decree-Law makes a crime
cards.body:
**Money laundering (Article 2):** dealing with the proceeds of crime to make their source look lawful, for example by:

- conducting a transaction with them,
- concealing or disguising their nature, source, location, movement or ownership,
- acquiring, receiving or transferring them, or
- keeping or possessing them,

while **knowing, believing or having reason to know or believe** they come from crime. Destroying evidence or helping an offender hide the crime counts as participation.

**Related offences (Article 2.6)** matter most to bank staff:

- failing to disclose information or suspicion gained through your work,
- ignoring or obstructing an order of the enforcement unit, and
- revealing an investigation or attachment order in a way likely to harm the investigation.

**Companies** can be fined and have property confiscated, and officers whose intent or gross negligence led to the offence are liable too.

cards.title: Which kind of offence is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each act into the category it falls under in Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001 as amended.

items.text: Buying a villa with bribe money while aware of where it came from
Splitting fraud proceeds across relatives' accounts to hide their source
A clerk keeps quiet about a suspicion he formed while processing a transfer
Telling a customer that an attachment order has been issued so he can move his money
Ignoring an order the enforcement unit obtained during an investigation
Collecting donations for a group known to carry out terrorist acts
Holding funds for safekeeping on behalf of a terrorist cell member

cards.title: Yusuf's secrecy question
cards.setting: Video call with Muharraq branch, 11:05 am.

lines.text: A long-standing customer says that if anyone asks about his account, banking secrecy protects him. Is he right?

Confidentiality matters, but the Decree-Law is clear on this point: a bank cannot plead secrecy before the investigating magistrate or the court for accounts, customer identity or records the law requires.
So if a lawful order comes in, we comply, through the proper channel.
Exactly. Requests go through the legal team and me, and we never tell the customer about an investigation.
That's clear. And what about the records he keeps asking us to delete?
We don't delete them. The law sets minimum retention periods. Let's look at the duties the law gives us.

cards.title: Article 5: what the law asks of every bank

cards.back: Keep a copy of each customer's identity evidence for five years after the relationship ends.
Keep a record of each transaction for five years after it was completed.
Report suspected transactions to the enforcement unit and the relevant authorities.
Give the enforcement unit any further information or help it asks for.
Follow the regulator's instructions on policies, procedures, management-level compliance officers and audit of those controls.
Never open or keep secret, fictitious or anonymous accounts.

cards.title: The lawyer's letter
cards.situation: An investigating magistrate's order asks Pearlgate for a customer's account records. The customer's lawyer then writes to Yusuf saying banking secrecy forbids the bank from handing anything over and asking whether 'something is going on'. Yusuf forwards it to you.

choices.text: Pass the order and the letter to the MLRO and legal team, comply with the order through them, and say nothing to the customer or lawyer about any investigation.
choices.outcome: Best. Under Article 7 of the Decree-Law a bank cannot plead secrecy against the magistrate or court for these records. Routing it through the MLRO keeps the response controlled, and silence avoids revealing an order in a way that could harm the investigation.

choices.text: Hold the records back until the customer's lawyer agrees in writing that they can be released.
choices.outcome: Poor. The customer's consent is not needed, and secrecy cannot be pleaded against the order. Delay could amount to obstructing an order, which is itself an offence.

choices.text: Comply with the order, but reply to the lawyer to reassure him that it is only routine.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Complying is correct, but commenting on the order to the customer's lawyer risks revealing it and prejudicing the investigation.

choices.text: Ask the branch team to send the records straight to the magistrate today to save time.
choices.outcome: Partly right on speed, but bypassing the MLRO and legal team risks sending incomplete records and loses the bank's audit trail of what was produced.

cards.title: How the framework grew
cards.caption: Laws and rules keep moving, so always check the current version before you rely on a paragraph number.

items.label: Decree-Law No. 4
items.detail: Bahrain's anti-money laundering law creates the offence, institutions' duties and the enforcement unit.

items.label: Module FC first issued
items.detail: First issued by the Bahrain Monetary Agency, the CBB's predecessor.

items.label: CBB replaces the BMA
items.detail: The CBB Law takes effect; the Rulebook modules stay in force.

items.label: Decree-Law No. 36
items.detail: Rewrites the terrorist financing offence in Article 3 with heavy penalties.

items.label: Mutual evaluation
items.detail: FATF approves Bahrain's mutual evaluation report in June 2018.

items.label: CBB guidance papers
items.detail: Guidance on terrorist financing, risk assessment and beneficial ownership.

items.label: Module FC amendments

cards.title: From the CBB's own reports: how AML supervision works
cards.body:
The CBB's annual reports describe its AML/CFT supervision in plain terms:

- The **Compliance Directorate** carries out onsite examinations of licensees to test compliance with the AML Law, the CBB Law and the Financial Crime Module, focusing on procedures, systems and internal controls.
- In 2021 it began producing **monthly sanctions exposure reports** to monitor the sector's exposure to major international sanctions programmes.
- Bahrain prepares regular **follow-up reports** on its mutual evaluation for the MENAFATF plenary; the 2021 report included requests to re-rate some FATF Recommendations.
- The CBB issued guidance papers on **risk assessment** and **beneficial ownership** in 2021 as part of its outreach to the industry.

The message for Pearlgate: an examination tests whether controls work in practice, not just whether a policy exists.

cards.title: Which version of Module FC are you reading?
cards.body:
The in-force CBB Rulebook is published on the CBB's Rulebook website, which this quest could not open automatically. Its Module FC content comes from **CBB-hosted copies**: the 2023 copies issued with the Module FC amendments and an earlier 2021 consultation copy, used only for sections whose 'date last changed' matches the 2023 contents list.

- Always check the paragraph in the current Rulebook before quoting it.
- Look at the **date last changed** printed for each section.
- Volume 1 covers **conventional banks**; other volumes cover other licensees and are not part of this quest.

cards.question: Which part of the CBB Rulebook holds the detailed AML/CFT rules for Pearlgate, a conventional bank licensee?
options: Module FC in Volume 1 (Conventional Banks)
The High-Level Controls Module in Volume 6
A separate AML regulation issued by the Ministry of Interior
The Policy Committee's reporting guidelines alone
cards.explanation: Module FC in Volume 1 applies to all conventional bank licensees and contains the CBB's directive on combating money laundering and terrorist financing. The Ministry of Interior's FIU receives reports; it does not issue the bank's rulebook.

cards.title: Stage 1 take-aways
items: Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001, as amended, creates the money laundering offence, related offences, penalties and banks' core duties.
Knowing, believing or having reason to believe funds are criminal is enough, and no conviction for the underlying crime is needed.
Failing to disclose a suspicion formed at work, obstructing orders or revealing an investigation are offences in their own right.
Banks must keep identity and transaction records, report suspicion, help the enforcement unit, run controls and never keep anonymous accounts.
Module FC in Volume 1 of the CBB Rulebook is the CBB's directive for conventional banks; check the current version of any paragraph.

cards.prompt: Think of one request you might receive at work that touches customer confidentiality, such as a court order or a relative asking about an account. Who in your bank should handle it, and what must you avoid saying to the customer?

quiz.question: Under Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001, which state of mind is enough for the money laundering offence when someone deals with proceeds of crime?
options: Knowing, believing or having reason to know or believe the property comes from crime
Only a written admission by the customer that the funds are criminal
Only proven, actual knowledge of the crime, confirmed beforehand by a final criminal court judgment
Only knowledge that the underlying crime took place in Bahrain
quiz.explanation: Article 2 covers knowing or believing, and also having reason to know or believe. The law defines criminal activity to include crimes in other states, so a Bahrain-only test is wrong.

quiz.question: A cashier at Pearlgate suspects a deposit is linked to drug trafficking but tells no one. What risk does the cashier personally face under the Decree-Law?
options: Committing a related offence for failing to disclose a suspicion formed in the course of employment
Only an internal warning from the bank, because the law's offences apply just to the customer and to people who handle the proceeds
None, because only the bank as a company can be prosecuted
None, because only the MLRO can commit offences under the law
quiz.explanation: Article 2.6 makes failing to disclose information or suspicion acquired through one's employment an offence related to money laundering. It applies to individuals, not only to the bank or the MLRO.

quiz.question: Which of these is a duty Article 5 of the Decree-Law places directly on institutions such as banks?
options: Approving the appointment of the members of the national Policy Committee
Not opening or keeping secret, fictitious or anonymous accounts
Prosecuting customers who launder money through their accounts
Publishing the names of customers reported to the authorities
quiz.explanation: Article 5 lists record keeping, reporting, cooperation, internal controls, audit and the ban on secret, fictitious or anonymous accounts. Prosecution belongs to the Public Prosecution, and naming reported customers would breach confidentiality and could tip them off.

quiz.question: For how long must a bank keep a copy of a customer's identity evidence under Article 5 of the Decree-Law?
options: Three years after the customer's last transaction
Five years after the relationship has ended
Five years after the account was first opened
Ten years after the customer's identity document expires
quiz.explanation: Article 5(a) runs the five-year period from the end of the relationship, not from opening. Transaction records run for five years after the transaction was completed.

quiz.question: A customer's lawyer insists that bank secrecy prevents Pearlgate from giving records to the investigating magistrate. What does the Decree-Law say?
options: Secrecy applies to foreign customers but not to Bahraini nationals
Secrecy prevails unless the customer gives the bank written consent to release the records to the magistrate
Secrecy can be pleaded once, after which the court decides on an appeal
Secrecy cannot be pleaded before the investigating magistrate or the court for these records
quiz.explanation: Article 7 removes the secrecy plea before the investigating magistrate and the competent court for accounts, customer identity and required records. Customer consent is not a condition.

quiz.question: Who does the Decree-Law make responsible for appointing the enforcement unit that receives money laundering reports?
options: The board of each licensed bank
The Minister of Interior
The Governor of the CBB
The Minister of Justice
quiz.explanation: Article 4.4 gives the Minister of Interior the power to appoint the enforcement unit, which receives reports, investigates and handles international cooperation. The CBB supervises banks but does not run the FIU.

quiz.question: Pearlgate's board asks whether the bank itself, not just individuals, can be punished for money laundering. What is the best answer?
options: Yes, but only through CBB administrative penalties under the Rulebook and never through the criminal courts
Only if the bank's chief executive personally carried out the transactions
Yes: the bank can be fined and lose property, and officers whose intent or gross negligence caused it are liable too
No: only natural persons can commit money laundering under Bahraini law
quiz.explanation: Article 3.3 provides for fines and confiscation against corporate bodies, and Article 2.5 makes officers acting for the body liable where the offence resulted from their intentional conduct or gross negligence.

quiz.question: Which body sets general anti-money laundering policies and issues guidelines on reporting suspicious transactions under Article 4 of the Decree-Law?
options: The Policy Committee
The bank's own internal audit department
The Public Prosecution
The CBB's Consumer Protection Office
quiz.explanation: Article 4 sets up a Policy Committee whose powers include setting general policies and issuing reporting guidelines in coordination with the relevant entities. The Public Prosecution conducts court proceedings.

quiz.question: Noora tells a new analyst to check the 'date last changed' next to each Module FC section. Why is that good practice?
options: Because sections that have not changed for more than five years no longer have legal effect for banks
Because the date shows when the bank last trained staff on that section
Because only sections changed in the current year are inspected by the CBB
Because the Rulebook is amended over time, so paragraphs must be checked against the current version
quiz.explanation: The CBB annotates each section with the date it last changed, and amendments such as the 2023 changes alter content. Old dates do not mean a rule has lapsed.

quiz.question: Which act would count as participation in money laundering under Article 2.2 of the Decree-Law?
options: Asking the customer about the purpose of a large outgoing transfer
Declining to open an account for a customer who refuses CDD
Destroying a document that could be used as evidence in the offence
Filing an internal suspicious transaction report with the MLRO
quiz.explanation: Article 2.2 treats destroying, concealing or forging potential evidence, or knowingly helping an offender hide the crime, as participation. The other options are normal compliance actions.

sessions.title: Risk-Based Approach and Customer Due Diligence under Module FC
sessions.summary: Apply the CBB's risk-based approach and the Module FC customer due diligence rules for conventional banks: what to collect and verify, beneficial owners, timing, incomplete CDD, non-resident customers and ongoing monitoring, including the BD 6,000 significant-transaction rule.
objectives: Explain the risk-based approach and the four risk categories the CBB expects banks to assess
Describe the information Module FC requires for natural persons and legal entities and how it is verified
Identify beneficial owners using the three-step test and apply the timing and incomplete-CDD rules
Apply ongoing monitoring rules, including how significant transactions are treated without automated monitoring

cards.title: Two customers at the gate
cards.setting: Pearlgate Bank, Muharraq branch. 9:40 am, a busy Sunday.

lines.text: Two arrivals this morning. An engineer who landed last week for a new job, still waiting for his CPR card, and two founders whose company is still being registered.
Both want accounts today. My team's instinct is to say 'come back when your papers are done'.
Module FC actually expects retail banks to help both of them, unless there are serious reasons not to. But there are conditions.
Like not letting money out until due diligence is complete?
That's one of them. And before any of that, we decide how risky each relationship is. Risk drives how deep we go.
Welcome to the Onboarding Gate. By the end of this stage you'll know what to collect, what to verify and when the door can open.

cards.title: The risk-based approach in five scenes

scenes.heading: Identify
scenes.narration: Start by listing the risks the bank faces. The CBB asks banks to look at country or geographic risk, customer risk, product, service and transaction risk, and delivery channel risk.

scenes.heading: Assess
scenes.narration: Next, judge how likely each risk is and how much harm it would cause. The CBB's guidance suggests a simple scale from low to significant.

scenes.heading: Evaluate
scenes.narration: Then decide priorities. Some risks need stronger controls; a few may be avoided altogether by not offering a product.

scenes.heading: Mitigate
scenes.narration: Apply controls in proportion to the risk: standard due diligence for most customers and enhanced measures where the risk is higher.

scenes.heading: Review
scenes.narration: Keep the documented risk assessment up to date, share it with senior management, and refresh each customer's risk profile through the relationship.

cards.title: Rating a risk: likelihood against impact
cards.caption: The CBB's risk assessment guidance uses likelihood and impact to rank risks. The same risk can rate differently in different banks.

items.label: Unlikely but severe
items.detail: Keep strong preventive controls and watch for change, for example sanctions exposure.

items.label: Likely and severe
items.detail: Significant risk: strongest controls, senior attention, possibly avoid the business.

items.label: Unlikely and minor
items.detail: Low risk: standard due diligence and routine monitoring.

items.label: Likely but minor
items.detail: Medium risk: tune monitoring and review more often.

cards.title: Which risk category?
cards.prompt: Sort each factor into the risk category the CBB's guidance places it in.

items.text: A country named by FATF as having weak AML/CFT systems
A country subject to UN sanctions or embargoes
A company with nominee shareholders or bearer shares
A cash-intensive business owner
A customer named in credible negative news about fraud
Private banking services
Accounts opened without meeting the customer face to face
Payments received from unknown, unrelated third parties

cards.question: The CBB's risk assessment guidance distinguishes inherent risk from residual risk. Which statement is correct?
options: Inherent risk is the level before any controls; residual risk is what remains after controls are applied
Inherent risk applies to customers; residual risk applies only to products
Residual risk is always zero once a bank has a written AML policy
cards.explanation: The guidance defines inherent risk as the natural level before mitigation and residual risk as what is left after it. A high residual risk suggests controls are not good enough and need remedial action.

cards.title: What to collect from an individual
cards.body:
Before providing **any** financial service to a natural person, Module FC requires a conventional bank to identify the customer and obtain, among other things:

- full legal name and other names used,
- full permanent residential address (a P.O. box is not enough),
- date and place of birth, nationality, passport number and CPR or Iqama number,
- occupation or public position, employer details,
- type of account and expected nature and volume of business,
- the customer's signature, **source of funds** and **reason for opening the account**.

**Verification (retail banks):** confirm name, date of birth and address through the **national E-KYC application**, or, where that is not practical, current official documents, with at least one copy showing a clear photograph.

Copies made from originals are certified by an authorised official writing **'original sighted'**, the date and a signature.

cards.title: Verifying identity: retail and wholesale banks
cards.caption: From Module FC sections FC-1.2.2A and FC-1.2.3 in the CBB-hosted 2023 copy.

items.label: Name and date of birth
items.left: National E-KYC application first; otherwise a current official document
items.right: A copy of a current, valid official identity document

items.label: Residential address
items.left: National E-KYC application first; otherwise a utility bill, statement or official record
items.right: A recent utility bill, bank statement, official record or home-visit record

items.label: Photograph
items.left: At least one copy shows a clear photograph
items.right: At least one copy shows a clear photograph

items.label: Extra step
items.right: Direct contact by phone, letter or email where appropriate

cards.title: Finding the beneficial owner of a company
cards.caption: Module FC requires banks to identify and take reasonable steps to verify beneficial owners of legal persons. The CBB's 2021 guidance explains the method.

items.label: Ownership
items.detail: Identify the natural persons who ultimately hold a controlling ownership interest.

items.label: Control by other means
items.detail: If ownership leaves doubt, or no one controls through ownership, find who controls by other means.

items.label: Senior managing official
items.detail: If no natural person is found, identify the person in the senior managing role.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Take reasonable measures to verify identities, and verify shareholders holding 20% or more.

cards.title: Onboarding a company customer
cards.prompt: Put Pearlgate's steps for a new corporate customer in the right order.
steps: Record the entity's details: name, registration number, legal form, addresses, activity and source of funds
Verify them with certified documents such as the commercial registration and constitutional documents
Work out the ownership structure and identify the beneficial owners, controllers and providers of funds
Verify the identity of beneficial owners and of shareholders holding 20% or more
Screen the entity, its owners and managers against sanctions lists and for PEP links
Rate the customer's risk and apply enhanced measures if the risk is higher
Approve the relationship and set up ongoing monitoring

cards.title: Anjali's alert
cards.setting: Transaction Monitoring team, head office. 2:15 pm.

lines.text: A small trading company opened with expected turnover of a few thousand dinars a month. This week it paid in BD 18,000 in cash in three visits.
What does our monitoring system say?
It flagged it as outside the expected profile. Module FC wants banks to verify the source of funds for significant or abnormal transactions and record what they found.
Right. And for banks without automated monitoring, the module sets a hard line: transactions above BD 6,000 count as significant and go in a daily report to the MLRO.
Do we just ask the customer, or does this go straight to an STR?
First we examine the background and purpose and document it. If the answer doesn't hold up, it becomes an internal report. Let's practise.

cards.title: The founders want their capital back
cards.situation: The two founders from this morning opened an account for their company under formation, with evidence that they applied for commercial registration. They deposited BD 50,000 of initial capital. Three days later, before the final registration or full CDD, they ask Yusuf to transfer BD 45,000 to a supplier abroad 'to secure stock'.

choices.text: Explain that the account can receive money but nothing can be paid out until registration and full CDD are complete, record the request, and tell the MLRO if the urgency or destination raises concern.
choices.outcome: Best. Module FC lets banks receive funds for companies under formation but bars disbursement until due diligence is complete. Recording the request and escalating concerns keeps the bank's options open.

choices.text: Make the payment because the account was opened properly and the money belongs to the company.
choices.outcome: Poor. Opening the account at stage one does not make it fully operational. Paying out before CDD is complete breaks the timing rules in Module FC.

choices.text: Close the account immediately and return the money in cash.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Exiting is an option where CDD cannot be completed, but these customers are still within the time allowed to finish their formalities, and funds received by transfer should be returned the same way.

choices.text: Allow a smaller payment of BD 5,000 as a goodwill gesture while the paperwork is finished.
choices.outcome: Poor. The rule is no disbursement until CDD is complete, whatever the amount. Splitting the payment does not change that.

cards.title: When due diligence cannot be completed

cards.front: Can we start before CDD is done?
cards.back: Generally no. A relationship or transaction must not start before CDD is complete, with narrow exceptions where no money may be paid out until CDD is finished.
Companies under formation being registered, newly arrived residents taking up work, non-face-to-face business, and documents submitted after initial CDD.

cards.front: CDD fails: what are the options?
cards.back: Consider freezing the funds and filing an STR, ending the relationship, not proceeding with the transaction, or returning the funds.
Return them by the method used to send them: cash for cash, wire for wire.
The person behind the account must be disclosed to the bank and verified.
Follow normal identification and also verify the parent or legal guardian.

cards.question: Pearlgate has no automated monitoring for one small product line. How must transactions above BD 6,000 on it be treated under Module FC?
options: They may be ignored if the customer is low risk
They must be reported to the FIU as STRs automatically
They are treated as significant, captured in a daily report for the MLRO or a delegate, and the records kept for five years
They must be approved by the CBB before processing
cards.explanation: Without automated monitoring, Module FC treats transactions above BD 6,000 as significant: they go into a daily report for the MLRO or a delegated official and the records are kept for five years. A large transaction is not automatically suspicious.

cards.title: Worked example: a non-resident customer file
cards.body:
A businessman living in another country asks Pearlgate's retail arm for an account. Module FC requires retail banks dealing with non-residents to have **documented acceptance criteria** and **approved policies** on what they offer them, backed by a risk assessment. Pearlgate's file therefore records:

- a **viable economic reason** for banking in Bahrain,
- **enhanced due diligence** results,
- his **country of tax residence**, where relevant,
- evidence of his **banking relationship at home**,
- an **indicative volume and value** of incoming funds, and
- a test that he can be **contacted without unreasonable delay**.

The bank also tells him which services, such as loans, credit cards or cheque books, may be limited because of his non-resident status. A file built this way lets Anjali's team spot activity that does not match the stated purpose.

cards.title: Keep CDD alive after onboarding
cards.body:
Due diligence does not end at account opening:

- **Scrutinise transactions** against what you know about the customer and their risk profile.
- **Investigate significant, unexpected or unexplained changes** in activity.
- When a customer **closes one account and opens another**, review and refresh their identity information.
- Standard terms must require customers to **provide up-to-date identification**.
- Review higher-risk customers more often, following your bank's documented review policy.

cards.title: Stage 2 take-aways
items: Assess country, customer, product or service and channel risk; document it, keep it current and match controls to the risk.
Collect the Module FC information set, including source of funds and reason for the account, and verify it, using E-KYC where practical.
For companies, identify beneficial owners by ownership, then control, then senior managing official, and verify shareholders of 20% or more.
No relationship or payout before CDD is complete; if CDD fails, consider an STR and freezing, exit, not proceeding or returning funds the same way.
Without automated monitoring, transactions above BD 6,000 are significant and go to the MLRO's daily report.

cards.prompt: Pick one customer type you deal with, such as salaried expatriates, small traders or new companies. Which of the four risk categories matters most for them, and what one extra question would help you understand their expected activity?

quiz.question: Which four risk categories does the CBB expect a conventional bank to assess in its ML/TF risk assessment?
options: Credit, market, liquidity and operational risk, as in the bank's prudential returns
Cash, cheque, card and wire transfer, split by transaction channel and value
Country or geographic, customer, product, service or transaction, and distribution channel
Retail, corporate, treasury and private banking
quiz.explanation: The CBB's risk assessment guidance and Module FC's risk-based approach both name country or geographic, customer, product, service or transaction, and delivery channel risk. The other lists describe prudential risks or business lines.

quiz.question: A retail customer can prove his address only with a post office box. What does Module FC say?
options: A P.O. box is acceptable if an employer letter confirms it
A P.O. box is acceptable if the customer is a GCC national
Addresses are optional for customers with a valid CPR
No: Module FC needs the full residential address
quiz.explanation: Module FC asks for the full permanent address, meaning the residential address, and states that a post office box is insufficient. Nationality or an employer letter does not change that.

quiz.question: How should an authorised Pearlgate official certify a copy of an identity document seen in original form?
options: Stamp it 'verified' and send it to the CBB for approval
Scan it without marking, since originals were seen
Write 'original sighted', the date and their signature
Ask the customer to sign the copy as a true copy
quiz.explanation: Module FC requires the official to write 'original sighted', with the date and signature, and equivalent measures for electronic copies. A customer's own signature is not certification.

quiz.question: A company's shares are spread so thinly that no natural person holds a controlling interest, and no one controls it by other means. Whom must Pearlgate identify as beneficial owner?
options: The company's external auditor
The natural person holding the senior managing official position
The largest corporate shareholder, whatever its own ownership
No one, because a company without a controlling owner has no beneficial owner
quiz.explanation: Module FC's cascade ends with the senior managing official where no natural person is found through ownership or other control. Leaving the field blank or naming a corporate shareholder does not meet the rule.

quiz.question: Which shareholders of a private company must Pearlgate verify under the Module FC due diligence rules, unless the company is a FATF/GCC listed company?
options: Shareholders holding 20% or more of the issued capital
Only shareholders who are also directors
Only shareholders resident outside Bahrain
Every shareholder, regardless of the size of the holding
quiz.explanation: Module FC asks banks to obtain and verify the identity of shareholders holding 20% or more of issued capital, where applicable, with an exception for FATF/GCC listed companies.

quiz.question: A new arrival awaiting his CPR asks to open a salary account. Under Module FC's timing rule, what is allowed?
options: Funds may come in before verification ends, but nothing may be paid out until CDD is met
The account may be used freely for 90 days, after which verification must be completed in full
The account must be refused until the CPR card is issued
The account can be fully used once the customer signs a declaration
quiz.explanation: Newly arrived persons taking up work or residence are one of the exceptions where verification can follow receipt of funds, provided nothing is disbursed until the requirements are met.

quiz.question: Pearlgate cannot complete CDD on a customer who sent BD 12,000 by wire transfer. Which option is consistent with Module FC?
options: Consider freezing and an STR, exiting, or returning the funds by wire
Return the funds in cash to close the matter quickly
Keep the account open and active, and complete the missing CDD at the next annual review
Process the customer's instructions and note the missing documents
quiz.explanation: Module FC lists freezing and filing an STR, terminating, not proceeding or returning funds by the same method. Funds received by wire go back by wire, not cash, and carrying on without CDD is not an option.

quiz.question: Anjali's monitoring flags a transaction that is large and outside a customer's normal pattern. What does Module FC require next?
options: Wait for a second unusual transaction before taking any action on the first one
Verify the source of funds, examine its purpose and record the findings
Block the customer's card and close the account
File an STR immediately without speaking to anyone
quiz.explanation: For significant or abnormal transactions, Module FC requires the bank to verify the source of funds, examine background and purpose and record the findings, with the investigation done by the MLRO or a delegate. An STR follows if suspicion remains.

quiz.question: Which item is part of the information Module FC asks a retail bank to obtain from a non-resident customer?
options: Approval of the account by the CBB's Compliance Directorate
A guarantee from a Bahraini citizen for the account
A deposit equal to six months of expected turnover
Evidence of a banking relationship in their home country
quiz.explanation: The non-resident rules include a viable economic reason, EDD, tax residence, evidence of home-country banking, reasons for using Bahrain, indicative volumes and contactability. Guarantees, deposits or CBB approval are not part of the list.

quiz.question: A customer closes his savings account and opens a new current account. What does Module FC require Pearlgate to do?
options: Nothing, because he is an existing customer
Review his identity information and re-verify anything missing or out of date
Treat the new account as a brand new customer relationship and file an STR as a precaution
Ask the CBB to confirm the customer's identity
quiz.explanation: Module FC requires a review of identity information when an existing customer closes one account and opens another, with missing or outdated information obtained and re-verified.

sessions.title: Enhanced Due Diligence: PEPs, Correspondents, Wire Transfers and TF Risk
sessions.summary: Apply Module FC's enhanced due diligence for higher-risk customers, politically exposed persons, non-face-to-face business, correspondent banking, introduced business, shell banks and wire transfers, and use the CBB's terrorist financing guidance to see why TF looks different from money laundering.
objectives: List the enhanced due diligence measures Module FC describes for higher-risk customers
Apply the PEP rules: identification, senior management approval, source of wealth and funds, and enhanced monitoring
Explain the extra steps for correspondent banking, shell banks, introduced business and wire transfers missing originator data
Contrast terrorist financing with money laundering using the CBB's 2020 TF guidance

cards.title: A busy morning in the harbour
cards.setting: Correspondent Banking and Trade desk, Pearlgate head office. 10:00 am.

lines.text: Two things on my desk. A small bank abroad wants us to be its correspondent for US dollar payments, and a private banking prospect turns out to be a senior official's brother.
Both are classic enhanced due diligence cases. Module FC has specific sections for each.
The relationship manager says the official's brother is 'just a businessman', so the PEP rules don't apply.
The PEP rules reach family members and close associates too. Being a relative is exactly the point.
And I have an inward transfer with no originator name or account number at all.
Then this is the right stage for all three of you. The High-Risk Harbour: where we go deeper before we go ahead.

cards.title: Enhanced due diligence in five scenes

scenes.heading: When it applies
scenes.narration: Module FC requires enhanced due diligence for customers identified as having a higher risk profile, with extra inquiries and information in their case.

scenes.heading: Know more
scenes.narration: That can mean more information about the customer and the purpose of the relationship, and updating their identification data more often.

scenes.heading: Follow the money
scenes.narration: It usually means understanding the source of funds and the source of wealth, and the reasons for particular transactions.

scenes.heading: Senior sign-off
scenes.narration: Senior management approval may be needed to start or continue the relationship.

scenes.heading: Watch closely
scenes.narration: Monitoring is stepped up, with more controls, more often, and closer review of selected transaction patterns.

cards.title: Handling a politically exposed person
cards.caption: Based on Section FC-1.5 as it appears in the CBB-hosted copy that could be opened; check the current Rulebook text.

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Use risk management systems and public databases to check PEP status at onboarding and periodically after.

items.label: Approve
items.detail: Obtain senior management approval before accepting a PEP as a customer.

items.label: Source of wealth and funds
items.detail: Record in the file the reasonable steps taken to establish both.

items.label: Profile
items.detail: Build a profile of expected activity to use in monitoring.

items.label: Monitor
items.detail: Apply enhanced ongoing monitoring, overseen at senior level such as by the MLRO.

items.label: Extend
items.detail: Apply the same rules to the PEP's family members and close associates.

cards.title: Which extra step fits?
cards.prompt: Match each higher-risk situation with a measure Module FC calls for.

pairs.right: Senior management approval before acceptance and a record of source of wealth and funds
A due diligence questionnaire, a signed statement of responsibilities and senior management approval

pairs.left: Account opened without meeting the customer
pairs.right: Extra measures to confirm the customer is who they claim and the address is genuine
A formal agreement, FATF-consistent CDD by the introducer and access to its records

pairs.left: Approach from a suspected shell bank
pairs.right: Refuse the relationship and make a suspicious transaction report

cards.question: The relationship manager says the PEP rules don't apply to the senior official's brother because the brother holds no public office himself. Who is right?
options: The relationship manager, because PEP rules apply only to office holders
Noora, because Module FC applies the PEP requirements to family members and close associates as well
Neither: relatives are covered only if they share a joint account with the PEP
The relationship manager, unless the brother is resident outside Bahrain
cards.explanation: Module FC extends the requirements for all types of PEP to their family and close associates. The brother needs the same enhanced measures, including senior management approval and source of wealth and funds.

cards.title: Correspondent banking under Module FC
cards.body:
Before Pearlgate acts as correspondent for a respondent bank, Module FC expects it to gather enough information, for example through a questionnaire, to understand the respondent's business. Factors include:

- ownership, management and main business activities,
- where it and its customers are located, and whether its country follows FATF standards,
- the strength of its AML/CFT controls and the purpose of the account,
- whether third parties use the account directly (payable-through accounts) and whether they were verified,
- whether it can provide customer identification data on request, and
- whether it has faced a money laundering or terrorist financing investigation.

Before opening, the bank must have a **signed statement** of each side's AML responsibilities and **senior management approval**. It must refuse relationships with **shell banks** and must not knowingly deal with banks that serve shell banks.

cards.title: How should Pearlgate respond?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation by the response Module FC points to.

items.text: A bank with no physical presence where it is licensed and no regulated group
A respondent bank that knowingly serves shell banks
A foreign minister's business partner opening a private banking account
A new correspondent relationship with a bank in a FATF-compliant country
A non-resident retail customer with income from abroad
A charity asking for an account before showing the ministry's certificate of authorised signatories
A resident teacher opening a salary account with expected activity
A resident engineer whose activity matches his stated salary

lines.text: This inward transfer has a beneficiary but no originator name, address or account number. Payments wants to credit it anyway.
It came through one of our correspondents. Maybe their system just dropped the fields.
Maybe. But Module FC tells us to scrutinise inward transfers missing originator information carefully, and to presume they are suspicious and pass them to the MLRO.
Unless the sending bank gives us the details quickly when we ask?
Yes: if it confirms the originator information in writing within two business days of our request, or the banks are acting as principals. Let's decide what to do.

cards.title: The wire with no sender
cards.situation: An inward transfer of USD 48,000 for a Pearlgate customer arrives without the originator's name or account number. The customer phones twice asking for the money and says the sender is 'a business friend'. The payments team wants to credit it now and chase the details later.

choices.text: Hold the transfer, ask the sending bank in writing for the originator information, and pass the case to the MLRO for review on a possible STR if the details do not arrive in time.
choices.outcome: Best. Module FC treats such transfers as presumed suspicious and sends them to the MLRO, unless the originating institution provides the information in writing within two business days of the request.

choices.text: Credit the funds because the beneficiary is a known customer with full CDD.
choices.outcome: Poor. Good CDD on the beneficiary does not fix missing originator information, which is what the rule targets.

choices.text: Ask the customer to tell you who sent the money and credit it if the answer sounds reasonable.
choices.outcome: Partly right. The customer's explanation is useful context, but the rule looks to the originating institution for the information, and discussing suspicion with the customer risks tipping off.

choices.text: Return the transfer immediately without telling anyone.
choices.outcome: Poor. Returning it may lose the information trail and skips the MLRO review the rule requires.

cards.title: Money laundering and terrorist financing compared
cards.caption: Drawn from the CBB's November 2020 guidance on combating the financing of terrorism and its 2021 risk assessment guidance.

items.label: Main purpose
items.left: Hide the criminal origin of funds
items.right: Get funds to terrorist acts, people or groups

items.label: Typical amounts
items.right: Often small and easy to overlook

cards.back: The three stages of terrorist financing: raising funds, moving them through channels, and using them for attacks, people or support.
Salaries, savings, businesses or charitable donations can all fund terrorism, so a clean source does not mean low TF risk.
A low-value transfer may be low risk for money laundering yet a TF warning sign alongside other factors.
The CBB's guidance notes that low-limit prepaid cards have been used for TF despite low ML risk.
Lawful funds such as charity collections can be diverted to radicalisation, recruitment or terrorism.
For UN designations, FATF reads 'without delay' as ideally within hours, to stop funds moving.

cards.question: Before opening a correspondent relationship for a respondent bank, which two steps does Module FC require?
options: A signed statement of each institution's AML responsibilities and senior management approval
A cash deposit from the respondent bank and approval by the CBB
A visit to the respondent's head office and a legal opinion from Bahrain
A guarantee from the respondent's central bank and annual audited accounts
cards.explanation: Module FC requires a signed statement setting out each institution's detection and monitoring responsibilities and senior management approval before the relationship opens. The other items may be useful but are not the stated requirements.

cards.title: Worked example: Pearlgate's file on a PEP
cards.body:
Pearlgate's private bank is asked to open an account for a former senior official from a neighbouring country who now runs a consultancy. The file shows how Module FC's PEP rules are applied:

- **Identification:** PEP status confirmed from public databases at onboarding, with a reminder to re-check periodically.
- **Approval:** the head of private banking and the MLRO sign off before acceptance, as senior management approval is required.
- **Source of wealth:** salary history, sale of a family property and the consultancy's audited accounts, recorded in writing.
- **Source of funds:** the first deposit comes from his own account at a regulated bank, matching the story.
- **Profile:** expected monthly inflows from consultancy fees and a few large investment transfers a year.
- **Monitoring:** enhanced monitoring with periodic senior review; his spouse and business partner are flagged as associates.

This is the quest's fictional story, not a real case.

cards.title: Stage 3 take-aways
items: Higher-risk customers need enhanced due diligence: more information, source of funds and wealth, senior approval and closer monitoring.
PEPs need identification at onboarding and periodically, senior management approval, a written record of source of wealth and funds, and enhanced monitoring; family and associates are covered.
Correspondent banking needs a questionnaire-based review, a signed responsibilities statement and senior approval; never deal with shell banks.
Inward wires missing originator data are presumed suspicious and go to the MLRO unless the sending bank supplies the data in writing within two business days.
TF can use small, clean-looking amounts; think 'raise, move, use' and do not rely on ML red flags alone.

cards.prompt: Which of today's higher-risk situations is most likely to reach your desk: a PEP, a correspondent, a non-face-to-face customer or an incomplete wire? Write down the first person you would escalate it to and what you would send them.

quiz.question: Which measure is listed in Module FC as part of enhanced due diligence for a higher-risk customer?
options: Senior management approval to start or continue the relationship
Waiving the need for a source of funds if the customer is wealthy
Reducing monitoring to avoid burdening a valuable client
Replacing identity checks with a personal reference only
quiz.explanation: Module FC's EDD measures include more information, source of funds and wealth, reasons for transactions, senior management approval and enhanced monitoring. EDD increases checks; it never removes them.

quiz.question: When must Pearlgate check whether a customer or beneficial owner is a PEP under Module FC?
options: Only when the customer makes a transaction above BD 6,000
Only once, when the account is opened
Only when the CBB sends a list of PEPs
At onboarding and periodically afterwards
quiz.explanation: Module FC requires risk management systems to determine PEP status both at the start of the relationship and periodically after it, using public databases and information. The CBB does not publish PEP lists for banks.

quiz.question: An existing Pearlgate customer is appointed to a senior government post. What does Module FC require?
options: Close the account, because banks may not keep relationships with serving government officials
Nothing, because PEP rules only apply to new customers
File an STR, because appointment to office is suspicious
Apply PEP measures, including senior approval to continue and enhanced monitoring
quiz.explanation: Where an existing customer becomes a PEP, Module FC requires enhanced measures, including a record of source of wealth and funds, senior management approval to continue and ongoing monitoring. Becoming a PEP is not suspicious in itself.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a factor Module FC lists for understanding a respondent bank in a correspondent relationship?
options: The respondent's ownership structure and management
The respondent's share price performance over the last five years
Whether the respondent has been subject to an ML or TF investigation
Whether the respondent can provide customer identification data on request
quiz.explanation: Module FC's factors cover ownership, management, activities, location, AML/CFT controls, account purpose, payable-through users, ability to supply customer data and past investigations. Share price performance is not one of them.

quiz.question: Pearlgate is approached by an institution it suspects is a shell bank. What must it do under Module FC?
options: Decline politely and take no further action
Open the relationship with enhanced monitoring
Refuse to establish relations and make a suspicious transaction report
Ask the institution's regulator for a reference and proceed if satisfied
quiz.explanation: Module FC bars relationships with shell banks and requires an STR when approached by a shell bank or a suspected one. Simply declining misses the reporting duty.

quiz.question: Pearlgate relies on an introducer for part of a customer's CDD. Who remains responsible for meeting Module FC's CDD requirements?
options: Pearlgate, not the introducer
The CBB, because it approves introducers
The introducer, once a formal agreement is signed
Responsibility is shared equally and split by contract
quiz.explanation: Module FC states that where part of CDD is delegated to another institution or intermediary, responsibility stays with the bank. The formal agreement and confirmations support, but do not transfer, that duty.

quiz.question: An inward wire lacks originator information. Under Module FC, when may Pearlgate avoid treating it as presumed suspicious?
options: If the sending bank supplies the details in writing within two business days of a request
If the beneficiary confirms by phone who sent the money and why it was sent to him
If the payment came through a correspondent in a GCC country
If the amount is below USD 10,000
quiz.explanation: The presumption lifts where the originating institution promptly, within two business days, supplies the information in writing on request, or where both banks act as principals. Amount, beneficiary statements or the route do not lift it.

quiz.question: According to the CBB's TF guidance, why can a small transfer be a TF warning sign even when it looks low risk for money laundering?
options: Because terrorist financing only ever involves transfers that fall below reporting thresholds
Because attacks may need little money, so small sums matter alongside other factors
Because all small transfers must be reported to the FIU
Because small transfers are always made in cash
quiz.explanation: The guidance explains that low-volume transfers may be lower ML risk but higher TF risk alongside other indicators, since attacks may need little money. It does not require reporting every small transfer.

quiz.question: Which description of terrorist financing stages matches the CBB's 2020 guidance?
options: Placement, layering and integration
Raise, move and use funds
Identify, assess and mitigate
Collect, verify and approve
quiz.explanation: The CBB's TF guidance describes raising, moving and using funds. Placement, layering and integration describe money laundering; identify-assess-mitigate describes risk assessment.

quiz.question: A charity asks Pearlgate to open an account. What must the bank have before providing financial services under Module FC?
options: A deposit guarantee from a licensed bank
A letter from the charity's chairman listing its main donors and the amounts they have given
A ministry-authenticated original certificate naming who may act for it
An STR filed in advance as a precaution
quiz.explanation: Module FC's EDD for charities, clubs and societies requires an original ministry-authenticated certificate identifying and authorising those acting for the organisation before services are provided.

sessions.title: Suspicious Transaction Reporting, Tipping Off, Terrorist Financing and Sanctions
sessions.summary: Follow a suspicion from the counter to the authorities under Module FC: internal reports to the MLRO, the MLRO's independent decision, external STRs through the online system to the FIU and the CBB, tipping off, the 2017 terrorist financing offence and the general duties on UN and CBB-designated persons.
objectives: Describe the internal and external STR process under Chapter FC-5, including who decides and how reports are sent
Recognise tipping off and the related offences under Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001
Explain the terrorist financing offence as rewritten by Decree-Law No. 36 of 2017
Describe in general terms the duties to screen, freeze and report for UN and CBB-designated persons

cards.title: A quiet word at the counter

lines.text: A teller, Salman, watches a customer pay in BD 9,500 in old notes for the third time this week, each time with a different story.
(visiting the branch) Salman, you look troubled. What's up?
Salman explains. His supervisor told him to 'leave it, he's a good customer, and the MLRO is too busy for small things'.
That's not how this works. Noora, can you join us?
(on the phone) Salman did the right thing by speaking up. A line manager can talk it through with him, but nobody can stop a report reaching me.
This is the Signal Room stage. Let's trace exactly what happens to Salman's suspicion, and what must never be said to the customer.

cards.title: From suspicion to STR in five scenes

scenes.heading: Notice
scenes.narration: Staff who handle customer business notice something they know or suspect is linked to money laundering or terrorist financing, or that simply looks unusual or suspicious.

scenes.heading: Report inside
scenes.narration: They report it promptly to the MLRO. Procedures can allow a chat with a line manager first, but that can never be used to stop the report.

scenes.heading: MLRO decides
scenes.narration: The MLRO, or an authorised delegate, considers the report with all the information the bank holds. The decision to report is not subject to anyone else's approval.

scenes.heading: Report outside
scenes.narration: If suspicion remains, the MLRO reports promptly through the online STR system to the financial intelligence unit at the Ministry of Interior and to the CBB's Compliance Directorate. Paper reports are not accepted.

scenes.heading: Stay silent and keep records
scenes.narration: Nobody tells the customer. If no report is made, the MLRO records why, and STR details are kept for at least five years.

cards.title: Salman's suspicion, step by step
cards.prompt: Put the reporting steps in the order Module FC sets them out.
steps: Salman notices unusual cash deposits that don't fit the customer's profile
Salman reports his suspicion promptly to the MLRO, using the internal procedure
The MLRO considers the report against all the information the bank holds
The MLRO decides, without needing anyone's consent, that suspicion remains
The MLRO files the STR through the online STR system to the FIU and the CBB's Compliance Directorate
The bank keeps the STR details and how it was handled for at least five years

cards.title: How alerts become STRs
cards.caption: Not every alert is suspicious, but every internal report gets a recorded decision.

items.label: Alerts and observations
items.detail: Monitoring alerts and things staff notice at the counter and in operations.

items.label: Internal reports
items.detail: Staff knowledge or suspicion reported promptly to the MLRO.

items.label: MLRO review
items.detail: Considered with KYC and all other relevant information the bank holds.

items.label: External STRs
items.detail: Filed online to the FIU and the CBB Compliance Directorate when suspicion remains.

cards.question: Salman's supervisor wants to discuss the case before it goes to the MLRO. What does Module FC say about this?
options: The supervisor decides whether the report goes ahead
Consultation is allowed, but it must not be used to stop a report reaching the MLRO
Consultation with line managers is prohibited in all cases
The teller must first get the customer's explanation in writing
cards.explanation: Module FC allows internal processes where staff consult line managers first, but these must not prevent reports reaching the MLRO once staff have stated knowledge or suspicion. Procedures must also allow disciplinary action against staff who fail to report without reasonable excuse.

cards.title: Tipping off and the related offences
cards.body:
Module FC states that, in line with the AML Law, the bank, its directors, officers and employees **must not warn or inform** customers, beneficial owners or other subjects that information about them is being reported.

It also says that if staff form a suspicion and believe that carrying on with CDD would **tip off** the customer, the bank may stop the CDD process and **must file an STR**.

Decree-Law No. 4 of 2001 backs this up with related offences:

- **failing to disclose** a suspicion gained at work,
- **obstructing** an order issued by or for the enforcement unit, and
- **disclosing** an investigation or attachment order in a way likely to harm the investigation.

In practice: no hints, no 'friendly warnings', no telling the customer why a payment is delayed beyond what your procedure allows.

cards.title: Tipping-off risk or safe practice?
cards.prompt: Sort each response to a suspicious customer.

items.text: 'Compliance has flagged you, so you might want to use another bank.'
Telling the customer an STR has been filed so he isn't surprised
Hinting that 'smaller deposits would attract less attention'
Mentioning to the customer's relative that the account is being looked at
Asking normal questions about the purpose of a transaction
Following the procedure's standard script for a delayed payment
Stopping further CDD questions that would alert him, and filing an STR
Escalating to the MLRO and saying nothing more to the customer

lines.text: Our screening tool has stopped an outgoing transfer. The beneficiary's name and date of birth match a person on a list the CBB circulated.
The customer is a trading firm I know well. Could it be a false positive?
It could. That's why we check identifiers properly. But until we know, the payment does not move.
Module FC says banks must not deal with persons the CBB designates and must report dealings using the STR procedure.
And then we follow any directions the authorities give. Let's work through the decision.

cards.title: The screening match
cards.situation: Pearlgate's screening holds an outgoing USD 120,000 transfer from a long-standing trading customer. The beneficiary's name, nationality and date of birth match an individual on a list of designated persons circulated by the CBB. The customer's finance director calls, asking why the payment is late and saying the deal will collapse.

choices.text: Keep the payment stopped, verify the match with the MLRO, and if it is confirmed report it through the STR procedure and follow the authorities' directions, telling the customer only what the procedure allows.
choices.outcome: Best. Module FC bars dealing with CBB-designated persons, requires reporting of any dealings through the FC-5.2 procedure and compliance with later directions. Careful wording avoids tipping off.

choices.text: Release the payment because the customer is long-standing and the match might be a coincidence.
choices.outcome: Poor. Releasing funds before the match is resolved risks making funds available to a designated person, which the sanctions rules are designed to prevent.

choices.text: Explain to the finance director that the beneficiary appears on a terrorist list so he can fix the paperwork.
choices.outcome: Poor. Disclosing the reason alerts the parties and may prejudice any action by the authorities.

choices.text: Cancel the payment and return the funds to the customer's account without escalating, since nothing left the bank.
choices.outcome: Partly right on stopping the payment, but it skips verification and reporting. The authorities need to know about attempted dealings with designated persons.

cards.title: Two kinds of sanctions screening
cards.caption: The CBB's TF guidance expects documented procedures for both types of screening, timely list updates and reporting of positive matches.

items.label: When
items.left: At onboarding and through the relationship

items.label: Must stay current
items.left: Lists updated for new listings and de-listings
items.right: Lists updated for new listings and de-listings

cards.title: Sanctions and terrorist financing: key points

cards.back: Banks must implement UN Security Council resolutions on terrorism and freeze the funds of persons and entities designated under them, without delay.
The CBB circulates lists of designated persons and entities; banks check for any dealings and report their findings.
Report accounts or dealings with designated persons using the STR procedure and follow later directions.
Funding a terrorist group or individual, or holding their funds, knowing of their terrorist activity, carries life imprisonment or at least 10 years.
Decree-Law No. 36 of 2017 set fines from BD 100,000 to BD 500,000 for the offence.
CBB guidance links PF risk to UN sanctions on the DPRK and Iran and to evasion through front companies.

cards.title: Reporting rules at a glance
cards.prompt: Match each situation to what Module FC says about it.

pairs.right: Not accepted: reports go through the online STR system
Must also be reported if suspicious, even if it never went through
Still reportable: the duty applies whether or not tax matters are involved
The reasons must be documented
Kept for at least five years

cards.question: Where must Pearlgate's MLRO send an external STR under Module FC?
options: To the CBB's Consumer Protection Office by email
To the Public Prosecution in writing
Through the online STR system to the FIU at the Ministry of Interior and the CBB's Compliance Directorate
To the customer's relationship manager for sign-off first
cards.explanation: Module FC sends external reports to the financial intelligence unit at the Ministry of Interior (named the Financial Intelligence Directorate in the Rulebook text) and to the CBB's Compliance Directorate through the online STR system. Paper reports are refused and no one else approves the MLRO's report.

cards.title: Worked example: the STR that nearly stalled
cards.body:
Salman's internal report reaches Noora at 1 pm. She checks the customer's profile: a self-employed tailor with expected deposits of around BD 1,500 a month. Three cash deposits of BD 9,500 in a week, in old notes, with inconsistent explanations, do not fit.

She pulls the account history, the CDD file and the branch's notes. There is no new business, no property sale and no inheritance on file. She concludes suspicion remains and files through the online STR system the same afternoon.

She also:

- records her reasoning and the evidence she reviewed,
- reminds the branch not to discuss the matter with the customer,
- asks HR to address the supervisor's attempt to block the report, as Module FC requires disciplinary arrangements for failures to report, and
- adds the case to her figures for the annual review of internal and external reports.

This is the quest's fictional story.

cards.title: Stage 4 take-aways
items: Staff report knowledge or suspicion promptly to the MLRO; line-manager consultation can never block a report.
The MLRO decides independently, files online to the FIU and the CBB Compliance Directorate, and documents reasons when not filing.
Report attempted transactions too, whether or not tax is involved, and keep STR details for at least five years.
Never tip off; if CDD would alert the customer, stop it and file an STR.
Do not deal with UN or CBB-designated persons; freeze without delay, report through the STR procedure and follow the authorities' directions.

cards.prompt: Imagine a customer asks you directly, 'Is there a problem with my account?' after you have escalated a suspicion. Write the words you would use that are honest, follow your bank's procedure and do not tip them off.

quiz.question: Which staff does Module FC require to report knowledge or suspicion promptly to the MLRO?
options: Only branch managers and above
Only staff in the compliance department
Staff who handle customer business and their managers
Only staff who have completed a specialist AML qualification
quiz.explanation: Section FC-5.1 covers staff who handle customer business or manage such staff. Limiting reporting to compliance or senior staff would leave the front line, where suspicion usually arises, out of the process.

quiz.question: What must a bank's internal reporting procedures include under Module FC, besides the route to the MLRO?
options: A cap on the number of reports each branch may make
A requirement for two managers to approve each internal report
Discipline for staff who fail to report without good excuse
A rule that reports are only made after the customer is interviewed
quiz.explanation: Module FC requires internal procedures to include disciplinary arrangements for staff who fail to report without reasonable excuse. Approval layers or customer interviews could block or tip off.

quiz.question: The MLRO reviews an internal report and decides not to file an STR. What must happen?
options: The case must be sent to the CBB for a second opinion
The MLRO documents why no report was made
The member of staff who raised it must sign to agree
The report is deleted to protect the customer
quiz.explanation: Module FC requires the MLRO to document why no external report was made. These records also feed the review of internal reports that did not become STRs.

quiz.question: A deputy general manager tells the MLRO that an STR on a major client needs the chief executive's approval. Is that right?
options: No: the MLRO's report needs no one else's consent
Yes, if the client's balances exceed a set threshold
Yes: STRs on major clients always need chief executive approval
No: the board must approve it instead of the chief executive
quiz.explanation: Module FC requires banks to ensure that where the MLRO or delegate suspects ML or TF, the report is made without being subject to the consent or approval of any other person.

quiz.question: A customer abandons a transfer when asked about its purpose, and the explanation offered was implausible. Must Pearlgate consider reporting it?
options: Yes: suspicious attempted transactions must be reported too
No: abandoned transactions are only noted in the customer file
Only if the amount exceeds BD 6,000
No: only completed transactions can be reported
quiz.explanation: Section FC-5.2 requires banks to report all suspicious transactions or attempted transactions. The BD 6,000 figure is a monitoring rule, not a reporting threshold.

quiz.question: While carrying out CDD, a relationship manager realises that further questions would alert the customer to a suspicion. What does Module FC allow?
options: Close the account and explain the bank's concerns
Stop pursuing the CDD process and file an STR
Wait until the next periodic review to raise it
Continue the questions but tell the customer they are routine
quiz.explanation: Module FC lets the bank choose not to pursue CDD where it reasonably believes that doing so would tip off the customer, but it must then file an STR.

quiz.question: Under Decree-Law No. 36 of 2017, which act is covered by the rewritten terrorist financing offence?
options: Holding a terrorist group member's funds for safekeeping, knowingly
Refusing to open an account for a charity without a ministry certificate
Failing to update a customer's address after a move
Filing an STR that later proves unfounded
quiz.explanation: The 2017 text covers collecting, contributing or allocating funds for terrorist groups or individuals, and obtaining their funds for safekeeping or use in their interest, with knowledge of their terrorist activity.

quiz.question: What does Module FC require when a bank finds it has accounts or dealings with persons designated by the CBB?
options: Close the account and pay the balance to the customer
Report them through the STR procedure and follow later directions
Ask the customer to confirm in writing that he is not a terrorist
Continue the relationship but monitor it more closely
quiz.explanation: Section FC-8.3 requires banks not to deal with CBB-designated persons, to report accounts or dealings through the FC-5.2 procedure and to follow later directions. Paying out the balance could make funds available to a designated person.

quiz.question: According to the CBB's TF guidance, what is the difference between customer screening and transaction screening?
options: Customer screening is optional for retail banks; transaction screening is mandatory
Customer screening uses CBB lists; transaction screening uses only internal lists
There is no difference; the terms describe the same control
Customer screening checks who the bank serves; transaction screening checks payments
quiz.explanation: The guidance describes two main controls: customer screening at onboarding and through the lifecycle, and transaction screening to catch payments involving targeted persons. Both need current lists.

quiz.question: How long must Pearlgate keep the relevant details of STRs it has submitted?
options: At least one year
